# Summary

Here we attempt to build a classification model that predicts whether an Ontario bridge needs rehabilitation soon, defined as having a Bridge Condition Index (BCI) below 70, the threshold of “good” condition, below which maintenance is usually scheduled within five years. We compared a baseline model, logistic regression and a radial basis function support vector classifier (RBF SVC) using cross-validation. On unseen test data, our final classifier, weighted RBF SVC, correctly identified 80 of the 98 bridges needing rehabilitation (recall of 0.82). However, only 38% of the bridges it flagged actually needed rehabilitation, giving an F1 score of 0.52. This means the model catches most bridges at risk but produces many false alarms, which would cost inspection time and money. Given these results, the model could help prioritize bridges for inspection, but should not replace inspections. Further work with more recent data and additional factors, such as traffic and climate, is needed before it could be used in practice.

# Methods
## Data
The dataset used for this project comes from the Government of Ontario. It was sourced from the Data Catologue and can be found [here](https://data.ontario.ca/dataset/bridge-conditions).

```{python}
# create data folders if they don't exist
os.makedirs("../data/raw", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs("../data/processed", exist_ok=True)

# download data
url = "https://data.ontario.ca/datastore/dump/703cdf01-ff09-4b86-b017-6e8d87b11fd2?bom=True"

# Write to file
request = requests.get(url)
with open("../data/raw/bridge_data_raw.csv", 'wb') as f:
    f.write(request.content)

# Load the raw data
raw_df = pd.read_csv('../data/raw/bridge_data_raw.csv')

# Filter for Bridges only
processed_df = raw_df[raw_df['CATEGORY'] == 'Bridge']

# Rename to use snake case for consistency
rename_map = {
    "ID (SITE Ndeg)": "site_id",
    "STRUCTURE NAME": "structure_name",
    "FRENCH NAME": "french_name",
    "HIGHWAY NAME": "highway_name",
    "LATITUDE": "latitude",
    "LONGITUDE": "longitude",
    "CATEGORY": "category",
    "SUBCATEGORY 1": "subcategory",
    "TYPE 1": "structure_type",
    "MATERIAL 1": "material",
    "YEAR BUILT": "year_built",
    "LAST MAJOR REHAB": "last_major_rehab",
    "LAST MINOR REHAB": "last_minor_rehab",
    "NUMBER OF SPAN / CELLS": "num_spans_cells",
    "SPAN DETAILS (m)": "span_details_m",
    "DECK / CULVERTS LENGTH (m)": "length_m",
    "WIDTH TOTAL (m)": "width_m",
    "REGION": "region",
    "COUNTY": "county",
    "OPERATION STATUS": "operation_status",
    "OWNER": "owner",
    "LAST INSPECTION DATE": "last_inspection_date",
    "CURRENT BCI": "current_bci",
}

processed_df = processed_df.rename(columns=rename_map)

# Drop rows that don't have a CURRENT_BCI (target), 52 rows
processed_df = processed_df.dropna(subset=['current_bci'])

# Create target variable
processed_df['rehab_soon'] = (processed_df['current_bci'] < 70).astype(int)

# Parse span_details_m into total, count, max, mean, and std
def extract_span_summary(val):
    """Helper function to parse span details into total,
    count, max, mean, and std span
    """
    txt = str(val).strip()
    t_match = re.search(r"Total\s*=\s*([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", txt, re.IGNORECASE)
    spans = [
        float(m.group(2))
        for m in re.finditer(r"\(\s*(\d+)\s*\)\s*=\s*([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", txt)
    ]

    if spans:
        arr = np.array(spans, dtype=float)
        total_val = (
            float(t_match.group(1))
            if t_match and float(t_match.group(1)) > 0
            else float(arr.sum())
        )
        return pd.Series(
            [total_val, float(len(arr)), float(arr.max()), float(arr.mean()), float(arr.std(ddof=0))]
        )

    try:
        num = float(txt.rstrip("mM "))
        return pd.Series([num, 1.0, num, num, 0.0])
    except ValueError:
        total_val = float(t_match.group(1)) if t_match else np.nan
        return pd.Series([total_val, 0.0, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan])


processed_df[['span_total_m', 'span_count', 'span_max_m', 'span_mean_m', 'span_std_m']] = (
    processed_df['span_details_m'].apply(extract_span_summary)
)

# Group together materials
low_count_materials = [
    'Unknown',
    'Engineered Wood (Psl, etc.)',
    'Mass Concrete',
    'Plastic/Geogrid/Geocell',
    'Glue Laminated Wood',
    'Masonry/Block/Rock'
]
processed_df['material'] = processed_df['material'].replace(low_count_materials, 'Other')

# Feature Engineering
processed_df['age'] = 2020 - processed_df['year_built']

processed_df['years_since_last_rehab_major'] = 2020 - processed_df['last_major_rehab'].fillna(processed_df['year_built'])
processed_df['years_since_last_rehab_minor'] = 2020 - processed_df['last_minor_rehab'].fillna(processed_df['year_built'])


# Columns to drop
drop_columns = [
    'category',
    '_id',
    'site_id',
    'structure_name',
    'french_name',
    'highway_name',
    'latitude',
    'longitude',
    '2020', '2019', '2018', '2017', '2016', '2015', '2014', '2013', '2012',
    '2011', '2010', '2009', '2008', '2007', '2006', '2005', '2004', '2003',
    '2002', '2001', '2000',
    'year_built',
    'last_major_rehab',
    'last_minor_rehab',
    'num_spans_cells',
    'span_details_m',
    'last_inspection_date'
]
processed_df = processed_df.drop(columns=drop_columns)
# Save the processed dataframe
processed_df.to_csv('../data/processed/bridge_data_processed.csv', index=False)
```

)

```{python}
# current_bci is dropped because the target was created from it (leakage).
X_train = train_df.drop(columns=["rehab_soon", "current_bci"])
y_train = train_df["rehab_soon"]

X_test = test_df.drop(columns=["rehab_soon", "current_bci"])
y_test = test_df["rehab_soon"]
```
```{python}
# Feature groups
numeric_features = [
    "age",
    "years_since_last_rehab_major",
    "years_since_last_rehab_minor",
    "length_m",
    "width_m",
    "span_total_m",
    "span_count",
    "span_max_m",
    "span_mean_m",
    "span_std_m",
]

categorical_features = [
    "material",
    "structure_type",
    "subcategory",
    "region",
    "owner",
    "operation_status",
]

drop_features = [
    "county",  # many small groups, a lot of null values
]
```
```{python}
num_pipe = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    StandardScaler()
)

cat_pipe = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"),
    OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)
)

bridge_preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (num_pipe, numeric_features),
    (cat_pipe, categorical_features),
    ("drop", drop_features),
     verbose_feature_names_out=False
)
```

# Results

```{python}
models = {
    "Baseline (most frequent)": (
        DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
        {},
    ),
    "Logistic Regression": (
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
        {
            "logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
            "logisticregression__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],
        },
    ),
    "RBF SVC": (
        SVC(),
        {
            "svc__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100],
            "svc__gamma": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1],
            "svc__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],
        },
    ),
}

grid_searches = {}
rows = []

for name, (model, grid) in models.items():
    search = GridSearchCV(
        make_pipeline(bridge_preprocessor, model),
        grid,
        cv=5,
        scoring="f1",
        return_train_score=True,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    grid_searches[name] = search

    best = search.best_index_
    rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Mean train F1": search.cv_results_["mean_train_score"][best],
        "Mean validation F1": search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"][best],
        "Best settings": search.best_params_,
    })

comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model")
comparison
```

```{python}
# RBF SVM had highest f1 score
best_model = grid_searches['RBF SVC']

y_pred = best_model.predict(X_test)

test_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "F1": [f1_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Recall": [recall_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Precision": [precision_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Accuracy": [accuracy_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)]
},)

test_scores
```

confusion.index = ["Actually needs rehab: No", "Actually needs rehab: Yes"]
confusion.columns = ["Predicted: No", "Predicted: Yes"]
confusion

# Discussion
Our final model, RBF SVC, showed moderate success at predicting whether an Ontario bridge needs rehabilitation soon (has a BCI below 70). On the test set it identified 82% of the bridges below this threshold, but only 38% of the bridges it flagged actually had a BCI below 70 (Table 7). The model outperformed the baseline’s 0% recall of bridges needing rehabilitation and an F1 score of 0 (Table 1).

These results suggest a model like this could be used to help prioritize which bridges to inspect or budget for, but it is not a replacement for inspections. The 18 bridges that were missed might not be rehabilitated, leading to further deterioration and potentially higher repair costs. However, 16% of the bridges that did not need rehabilitation were still flagged. This would waste inspection time and money. Note that the BCI reflects a bridge’s physical condition, it does not predict the likelihood of failure of the bridge or safety (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021), so a missed bridge does not imply an unsafe one.

Some of these results were expected. Our EDA showed that bridges needing rehabilitation were older on average and had gone longer since their last major rehabilitation (Table 2), suggesting these features hold useful information about bridge condition. The low precision was also expected because the tuned models used balanced class weights, which push the model to flag more bridges in the minority class, which leads to higher recall of bridges needing maintenance at the expense of precision. The overall moderate performance despite some of these clear patterns was surprising. One possible reason is that bridges with a BCI just above or below 70 are hard to classify using structural features alone, and that factors not in our data, such as traffic volume, climate and maintenance history, also affect deterioration.

Several directions could be explored to improve the model. Examining misclassified bridges, particularly those with a BCI close to 70, could reveal which features drive misclassification. This is supported by previous work on the same Ministry of Transportation’s public bridge condition data, which found that the original attributes were not suitable for reliable classification models of future BCI, and that tuning the attributes was key to improving performance (Martinez et al. 2020). Adding environmental and usage factors not in our data, such as climate and traffic volume, and using each bridge’s condition history to forecast when its BCI is likely to fall below 70, could make the model both more accurate and more useful for planning. Finally, since logistic regression performed almost as well as the RBF SVC with less overfitting, examining its coefficients could show which bridge characteristics, such as age, material or region, most strongly drive deterioration.

Our analysis should be read with some assumptions and limitations in mind. We assumed that a BCI below 70 is a meaningful indication of a bridge needing work soon (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021). This means bridges either side of 70 are flagged differently even when their BMI is similar. In cleaning, we assumed that the missing rehabilitation year means a bridge was never rehabilitated. The data set reflects bridge conditions around 2020, and may not represent current conditions. Moreover, the data does not include factors that likely affect bridge conditions including climate and traffic volume. Finally, with only 98 bridges needing rehabilitation in the test set, results from a single train/test split are fairly uncertain, and they apply only to the bridges in this dataset, not to culverts or bridges elsewhere. More recent data with these additional factors would be needed to judge whether the model is useful in practice.
